question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6(b)(15), what buffer distance does Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act generally require along the banks of state waters, measured horizontally from the point where vegetation has been wrested by normal stream flow?
choice_a: A 100-foot buffer with no exceptions of any kind
choice_b: A 25-foot buffer within which land-disturbing activities are generally prohibited, subject to specified exceptions
choice_c: No buffer requirement exists under Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act
choice_d: A 5-foot buffer, applicable only to commercial development
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6(b)(15) establishes a 25-foot buffer along the banks of state waters, measured horizontally from the vegetation line, within which land-disturbing activities are generally prohibited -- subject to specific exceptions such as certain drainage structures and limited-width perpendicular utility crossings.

question: How does the required buffer along a designated trout stream compare to the standard state-waters buffer under Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act?
choice_a: Trout streams require no buffer at all, unlike other state waters
choice_b: Trout streams and all other state waters require the identical 25-foot buffer, with no distinction
choice_c: A trout stream requires a larger, 50-foot buffer, compared to the standard 25-foot buffer for other state waters (though small springs/streams with limited average annual flow may use a 25-foot buffer or be piped at the landowner's discretion)
choice_d: Trout streams require a smaller, 10-foot buffer than other state waters
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6(16) generally imposes a larger 50-foot buffer along designated trout streams, compared to the standard 25-foot buffer for other state waters -- though certain small springs or streams with limited average annual flow may use the smaller 25-foot buffer or be piped at the landowner's discretion.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6(17), what buffer applies along the coastal marshland-upland interface in Georgia?
choice_a: No buffer of any kind applies to coastal marshlands under the Erosion and Sedimentation Act
choice_b: A 50-foot buffer identical to the trout stream standard, with no exceptions
choice_c: A 500-foot buffer applicable to all coastal development
choice_d: A 25-foot buffer, with exceptions for maintenance activities and certain authorized alterations
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6(17) establishes a 25-foot buffer along the coastal marshland-upland interface, subject to exceptions for maintenance activities and certain authorized alterations -- a distinct buffer category from the standard state-waters and trout-stream buffers.

question: Under Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act, is a single-family home construction project generally exempt from the Act's land-disturbing-activity permitting requirements?
choice_a: Yes, generally, unless the land disturbance equals or exceeds five acres
choice_b: No -- single-family home construction is never exempt regardless of the size of the disturbed area
choice_c: Yes, without any size limitation whatsoever
choice_d: The exemption applies only to disturbances under one-tenth of an acre
explanation: Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act generally exempts single-family home construction from certain of its requirements, unless the land disturbance involved equals or exceeds five acres -- at which point the project falls back under the Act's standard requirements.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6, what defense is available to a developer facing a storm-water-discharge enforcement action if best management practices (BMPs) were properly designed, installed, and maintained?
choice_a: BMPs provide no legal defense of any kind, regardless of how well they were implemented
choice_b: Proper design, installation, and maintenance of BMPs constitutes a complete defense to such an enforcement action
choice_c: BMPs are relevant only to reducing (not eliminating) the amount of a fine, never a full defense
choice_d: The BMP defense applies only to commercial developments over 100 acres
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 12-7-6 provides that proper design, installation, and maintenance of best management practices constitutes a complete defense to an enforcement action concerning storm water discharge compliance -- incentivizing developers to implement BMPs correctly.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4, how much advance notice must a local government generally publish in a newspaper of general circulation before holding a public hearing on a zoning decision?
choice_b: At least 6 months before the hearing
choice_c: At least 15 days but not more than 45 days before the hearing date
choice_d: No advance notice period is specified under Georgia's Zoning Procedures Law
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4 requires published notice of a zoning public hearing at least 15 days but not more than 45 days before the hearing date, in a newspaper of general circulation.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4, when a rezoning is initiated by a party other than the local government itself, what must the published notice include beyond the basic time, place, and purpose of the hearing?
choice_b: A complete architectural rendering of any proposed structure
choice_c: The names of every property owner within a 5-mile radius
choice_d: The property's location, its current zoning classification, and the proposed zoning classification
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4 requires that, for a rezoning initiated by a party other than the local government, the published notice additionally include the property's location, its current zoning classification, and the proposed classification -- beyond the basic time/place/purpose notice required for government-initiated hearings.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4, when a rezoning is initiated by someone other than the local government, what physical sign requirement applies to the subject property before the hearing?
choice_a: A sign containing the information required by local ordinance or resolution must be placed in a conspicuous location on the property not less than 15 days before the hearing date
choice_b: No sign of any kind is ever required on the subject property
choice_c: The sign requirement applies only to government-initiated rezonings, never to privately initiated ones
choice_d: The sign must remain posted for a minimum of one full year after the hearing
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4 requires, for a non-government-initiated rezoning, that a sign with the locally required information be placed conspicuously on the subject property not less than 15 days before the hearing date, giving the public visible notice in addition to the newspaper publication.

question: A property owner's rezoning application is formally defeated by the local governing authority. Under O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4, how soon may the same property again be considered for rezoning?
choice_a: Immediately -- the owner may reapply the next business day
choice_b: Not until at least six months have passed following the defeat
choice_c: Not until at least five years have passed
choice_d: The property can never again be considered for rezoning once an application has been defeated
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4 provides that once a rezoning amendment is defeated, the same property may not again be considered for rezoning until at least six months have passed following the defeat -- a cooling-off period, though not a permanent bar.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4, what heightened procedural requirements apply to a zoning amendment that would authorize multifamily use on property currently zoned single-family?
choice_a: No heightened requirements apply -- multifamily rezonings follow the identical single-hearing process as any other rezoning
choice_b: A single hearing held on a Sunday morning is specifically required
choice_c: Two public hearings, held at least three months and not more than nine months before final action, with adoption occurring at two separate meetings not less than 21 days apart, and at least one hearing held between 5:00 and 8:00 P.M.
choice_d: Only a written petition signed by every adjoining property owner is required, with no public hearing at all
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-66-4 imposes heightened procedural safeguards for a single-family-to-multifamily rezoning: two public hearings held three to nine months before final action, adoption at two separate meetings at least 21 days apart, and at least one hearing scheduled between 5:00 and 8:00 P.M. to improve public accessibility.

question: Under Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act, at what turbidity increase (in nephelometric turbidity units, or NTUs) does storm water discharge from an improperly managed disturbed area generally trigger a separate daily violation in warm-water fisheries, as opposed to trout waters?
choice_a: The threshold is identical (10 NTUs) for both warm-water fisheries and trout waters
choice_b: 100 NTUs for warm-water fisheries, with no separate standard for trout waters
choice_c: There is no turbidity-based violation standard under the Act
choice_d: 25 NTUs for warm-water fisheries, compared to a stricter 10 NTUs for trout waters
explanation: Georgia's Erosion and Sedimentation Act sets separate turbidity-increase violation thresholds: 25 NTUs for warm-water fisheries, and a stricter 10 NTUs for trout waters, reflecting trout waters' greater sensitivity to sediment -- each qualifying discharge event constitutes a separate daily violation.

question: Under Georgia's Development Impact Fee Act, O.C.G.A. Section 36-71-4, what is the general limit on the amount of a development impact fee a local government may charge?
choice_a: The fee may not exceed a proportionate share of the cost of system improvements reasonably attributable to the new development, calculated by service area and adopted level of service
choice_b: There is no limit at all -- a local government may set any impact fee amount it chooses
choice_c: The fee is capped nationally at a flat $500 per building permit, regardless of the type or size of development
choice_d: The fee may exceed the proportionate cost of system improvements as long as the excess funds general government operations
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-71-4 limits a development impact fee to a proportionate share of the cost of system improvements reasonably attributable to the new development, calculated based on defined service areas and the jurisdiction's adopted level of service -- not an unlimited or flat-rate charge.

question: Under Georgia's Development Impact Fee Act, at what point in the development process are impact fees generally collected?
choice_a: At the closing of the final home sale to an end buyer, years after construction
choice_b: At the time of building permit issuance, with limited exceptions for certain public facilities
choice_c: Only after the entire subdivision has received its certificate of occupancy
choice_d: At the time the initial rezoning application is filed, before any building permit is sought
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-71-4 provides that development impact fees are generally collected at the time of building permit issuance, with limited exceptions for certain public facilities where different collection timing may apply.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 36-71-9, if a local government collects a development impact fee but fails to spend it on the applicable system improvements within a specified period, what generally happens to the unused fee?
choice_a: The local government may keep the unused fee indefinitely for any governmental purpose
choice_b: The developer forfeits any right to a refund automatically after 90 days
choice_c: If the fee remains unspent after six years, the local government must refund it (tracked on a first-in, first-out basis), including a pro rata share of interest actually earned, following required notice procedures
choice_d: Unused impact fees automatically convert into property tax credits for the entire county
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 36-71-9 requires a local government to refund an impact fee left unspent after six years (tracked FIFO), including a pro rata share of interest actually earned, after providing required notice to the property owner -- protecting developers from fees collected but never applied to the intended system improvements.

question: As a matter of general national zoning terminology, what is 'downzoning,' and how does it typically affect an affected property's use rights?
choice_a: Downzoning always increases the maximum density or intensity of use permitted on a property
choice_b: Downzoning refers exclusively to lowering a property's assessed tax value, unrelated to zoning classification
choice_c: Downzoning is a term used only for agricultural land and has no application to residential or commercial property
choice_d: Downzoning is a rezoning that reduces the permitted density or intensity of use on a property (such as changing multifamily zoning to single-family), typically decreasing the range of uses or development potential compared to the prior classification
explanation: Downzoning is a rezoning action that reduces a property's permitted density or intensity of use (e.g., rezoning from multifamily to single-family, or from commercial to a more restrictive classification), generally decreasing the property's development potential compared to its prior zoning.
source_note: hedge: standard national zoning terminology, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: As a matter of general national zoning doctrine, what is 'spot zoning,' and why is it generally viewed unfavorably by courts?
choice_a: Spot zoning is the rezoning of a small parcel in a manner inconsistent with the surrounding area's zoning and the jurisdiction's comprehensive plan, often benefiting a single owner without a legitimate public-interest justification -- courts often view it unfavorably as arbitrary or as improper special-interest legislation
choice_b: Spot zoning describes the standard, favored practice of rezoning an entire district uniformly
choice_c: Spot zoning refers only to the placement of directional street signage within a subdivision
choice_d: Spot zoning is a legally required step before any zoning ordinance may be adopted
explanation: Spot zoning involves rezoning an isolated, small parcel in a way inconsistent with the surrounding area's zoning and the jurisdiction's comprehensive plan, often perceived as benefiting a single property owner without adequate public-interest justification -- courts often scrutinize or invalidate spot zoning as arbitrary, capricious, or inconsistent with sound planning.
source_note: hedge: standard national zoning doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: As a matter of general national zoning terminology, what is an 'overlay district,' as distinguished from a standard base zoning district?
choice_a: An overlay district completely replaces the underlying base zoning district's regulations, eliminating them entirely
choice_b: An overlay district applies a supplemental set of standards or restrictions (such as historic-preservation, flood-hazard, or airport-noise requirements) on top of an area's existing base zoning district, without necessarily changing the underlying permitted uses
choice_c: An overlay district applies only to unincorporated county land, never to land within a city's limits
choice_d: An overlay district is simply another term for a variance
explanation: An overlay district layers additional, supplemental standards (such as historic preservation, floodplain, or airport-noise restrictions) on top of an area's existing base zoning, rather than replacing the base district's underlying use classifications -- properties in an overlay district must comply with both the base district's rules and the overlay's additional requirements.
source_note: hedge: standard national zoning terminology, not Georgia-statute-specific
